prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form, which made incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange my preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part B012 prize to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. All six of us reached it independently, and nobody's round-1 file weakened the scientific case. The chain from incretin physiology (Holst), through the biology of the proglucagon-derived peptides (Drucker), to identification of the insulinotropic GLP-1(7-36) form (Mojsov) is mechanistically complete, independently confirmed over decades, and validated in large randomized outcome trials with glycaemic, weight, cardiovascular and renal benefit. Nobody disputes maturity. In answer to the chair's first question, I would word the citation around the physiology and the active form of the hormone, and I would accept an accompanying explanatory text that says plainly that the long-acting agonists are a later pharmaceutical development and are not what is being rewarded. That keeps the prize about discovery and avoids implying that the three laureates made the drugs.
statement.case_against: The attribution weaknesses are real and round 1 did not remove them. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is contested against Habener and colleagues, who are not on the supplied credit list, and I cannot settle that from the files. Knudsen is credited on the ballot entry but excluded in all six configurations, and Sten and Rickard are right that protraction chemistry that turned a peptide with a half-life of minutes into a weekly medicine was a scientific achievement and not routine translation. If Mojsov's standing proved weaker than the record suggests, I would reopen the third name and consider Knudsen, but not at the expense of Holst or Drucker. A second risk is that unanimity makes us test this case less hard than a contested one.

responses.point: Thomas would keep Holst, Drucker and Mojsov, treats Knudsen's exclusion as defensible, and would not accept a configuration that includes Knudsen at the expense of the basic-science names; he also treats B024 as the preferred second part, with B016 as a fallback if the GLP-1 attribution stalls.
responses.response: I agree on the trio and on not trading Holst or Drucker for Knudsen. I am less comfortable than Thomas with calling the exclusion merely defensible, because the citation has to carry it openly. Where I differ is the fallback. If GLP-1 attribution stalled, I would not move to B016, since the oncogene biology sits outside the credited trio, as you say yourself. I would first reconsider the third GLP-1 name. On B024, Thomas's strongest point is that Walter and Mori is clean, but I still weigh the largely prospective disease payoff, so I would not add it as a second part this year.

responses.point: Rickard argues that B024 is the strongest purely mechanistic case, that B012 risks crowding it out, and that Knudsen could replace Mojsov if her priority proves weaker than the record suggests.
responses.response: I take the crowding-out concern seriously, and Walter and Mori remains a clean, well-confirmed pair, so I ranked it fourth and not lower. But a basic-discovery prize is not disqualified by the lack of translation; my reservation is that, set beside B012 in a shared prize, it would be a mechanism awaiting its disease payoff next to one that has already changed treatment, and the chair rightly notes that Ron and the PERK arm are not credited. I agree with Rickard that the Mojsov question is the point to test, and that Knudsen is the right person to consider if it fails, without widening to four names.

responses.point: Sten does not accept that B046 is the second alternative: the discovery step for TNF blockade is unclear to him, he would rank it behind B009 and B024, and he remains open if colleagues can show Feldmann and Maini's contribution was more decisive; he also holds that Eshhar's omission weakens B009.
responses.response: That is a fair challenge and I have to answer it rather than repeat my ranking. Feldmann and Maini showed that blocking one cytokine, TNF, could control a chronic autoimmune disease, and the mechanistic work on TNF as a driver in synovial tissue was tested clinically by the same pair. But the target biology, antibody engineering and industrial development all sit around them, and Perlmann and Svenningsson make the same point. That persuades me that B046 is a later-year candidate more than a rival to B012 now. On B009 I now agree with you and Rickard that Eshhar's omission is serious, and I have moved the two-name June and Sadelain version ahead of B046 as my first alternative.

responses.point: The chair keeps B016 above B046 and B009 on maturity, and asks in the summary whether, for B016 and B046, the deciding element is target biology or drug and clinical proof of concept.
responses.response: My answer to the chair's last question is that for B046 the deciding element was clinical proof that a single cytokine drives chronic disease. That is a real discovery, but it rests on target biology and engineering by others. For B016 it is the opposite problem: the clinical proof is overwhelming, but the Philadelphia chromosome and BCR-ABL discoveries are outside the credited names. Neither is a fit for this year's three-person limit, and I do not think either is a weak candidate. I therefore keep both outside the preferred configuration.

responses.point: Abdel asked which step was decisive for TNF blockade, showing TNF drives synovial inflammation or clinical proof of concept, and said he would raise B046 if it was the first.
responses.response: My honest answer is that both steps belong to Feldmann and Maini, but the clinical proof of concept is the part that changed medicine, and the mechanistic part rests on antecedents outside their credit. So I do not think it should rise above B012. I also agree with Abdel that a single-part prize with three basic-science names avoids splitting the award for balance, and I would not add a second part just to broaden the prize.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution to identifying the active GLP-1 peptide can be credited as independent of Habener and colleagues, which I cannot verify from the files.
Whether the committee will accept a citation that is explicitly about physiology and the active peptide while Knudsen's protraction work is left unrewarded.
Whether B009 in the two-name version can be settled given the missing Eshhar concept, and whether it is mature enough on durability and safety to be a second part in a future year.
Whether a single-achievement prize is better than a shared one, given that every candidate second part has a named credit or maturity problem.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict for the preferred configuration (B012). My field of autoimmunity and rheumatology is close to B046 (TNF blockade) and to the immune side of B009, but I have no documented personal or institutional connection to Feldmann, Maini, June, Sadelain or Rosenberg, and no change since round 1. I would recuse if a connection were identified. Shared institutional setting with other committee members is not a conflict.
